To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have built a model to classify schizophrenia patients and controls from structural MRI data that has a classification accuracy of 71% and that this accuracy can be reproduced in an independent validation sample.

we could build a model that can correctly classify 70% of the schizophrenia patients and healthy subjects in an independent sample, that the model's pattern of gray matter density differences is in line with previous findings, and that the model is stable, if built from a training sample of at least 130 subjects.
we have built a model that classifies schizophrenia patients and healthy subjects based on whole brain VBM data with 71% accuracy and we have replicated this result in an independent sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model that classifies schizophrenia patients and healthy individuals based on structural MRI scans.
the development of a diagnostic tool for schizophrenia based on VBM data.
developing and validating a method to classify schizophrenia patients and controls based on whole-brain gray matter density maps derived from structural magnetic resonance images.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model can be used to classify schizophrenia patients and control subjects, but that the classification accuracy is not sufficiently high for a clinical use.
we have demonstrated the feasibility of using structural MRI scans to classify schizophrenia patients and controls, but that further studies are needed before this can be used in clinical practice.
the model presented here is not a diagnostic test for schizophrenia, but that the model is able to distinguish schizophrenia patients from healthy controls based on gray matter densities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the model we developed is stable and can classify schizophrenia patients from healthy controls with an accuracy of approximately 70%.
the model can be considered stable, if the training sample is larger than 130 subjects.
a model built with 239 subjects classified 71.3% correct (leave-one-out) and when applied to an unaltered independent test sample of 277 individuals, the model classified 70.4 % correct.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to classify schizophrenia patients and controls with a reasonable accuracy using structural MRI scans and a simple machine learning algorithm.

classification of schizophrenia patients and controls from structural MRI data is possible, even when using a relatively small number of subjects, and that this classification can be used as a tool to investigate brain abnormalities associated with the disorder.
